summary:
Perlis stands under Malaysia's federal Penal Code 1936. Sections 377A and 377B punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, and the Human Dignity Trust country profile (last updated 16 December 2025) records offences of gross indecency alongside them, each carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian nationals and reach visitors present in Perlis.

The state layer applies only to Muslims. Perlis is one of all 13 states, together with Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, that maintain Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Since the 1980s every state has passed such an enactment and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. A non-Muslim foreign visitor is not exposed to this layer; the federal offences are.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, so a trans visitor whose identity documents do not match their presentation has no domestic mechanism to rely on. The Human Dignity Trust profile further records that discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is public and organised. The Religious Affairs Minister stated in July 2020 that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

The documented pattern of exposure is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. A crackdown has been under way since the 2018 election: an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced at least 20 LGBT arrests, an August 2022 raid on an LGBT venue detained twenty men, a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned, and in November 2023 Johor authorities announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B; media had been pre-tipped, detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended, and 31 foreign nationals were held until their embassies intervened. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground. Police raided a second sauna in Penang days later.

Trans people in Malaysia also face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor in Perlis, enforcement against consenting adults in private remains uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but venue raids carry acute exposure risk, including for foreign nationals held in them.
tangentialFactors:
Court rulings have shifted authority between the two legal layers rather than decriminalising anything. The Federal Court's February 2021 decision on Selangor's section 28 and its February 2024 decision on 16 Kelantan provisions rested on federalism grounds, and the earlier High Court refusal to declare the cross-dressing ban unconstitutional left the state offence in place; through all of it the federal Penal Code offences stood unchanged.

The enforcement climate is directed at LGBT people generally, not only at trans people. Arrests at a Halloween party and at an LGBT venue, the caning sentence imposed on a lesbian couple by a Terengganu Sharia court, Johor's conversion-therapy centre plans and censorship of LGBT events and media content all sit alongside the cross-dressing offences and the sauna raids, so the visitor-facing risk is a broadened enforcement posture rather than a single trans-specific provision.

Reform prospects are foreclosed by Islamist opposition, and Malaysia has neither same-sex marriage nor a general anti-discrimination law to fall back on.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 for their August 2022 report on conversion practices, discrimination and violence, a national evidence base that sets the frame for Perlis; neither source identifies a Perlis-specific enforcement case.
localsOnly:
Muslim residents of Perlis are exposed to the state cross-dressing offence, which carries up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, enforced by the state Islamic religious department. Which enactments also bar women from posing as men is not stated for Perlis in the available sources.

Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees as of June 2021, and the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report of 10 August 2022 documents conversion practices applied to LGBT people from interviews conducted between 2018 and 2021.

Residents have no legal gender-recognition procedure available. LGBT events and media content are censored, no anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no recognition of same-sex partnerships.

Documentation of a trans woman's killing in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third such killing in under two months, records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself". Since the 2018 election the authorities have pursued raids, caning sentences and conversion-therapy initiatives against LGBT people in several states.
outOfScopeNotes:
Neither source names a Perlis-specific enforcement case, arrest or prosecution under the cross-dressing enactment, so the state-level enforcement picture here rests on the national pattern rather than local records.

Whether the Perlis Sharia enactment also criminalises women posing as men is unresolved in the available material, which states only that three of the 13 states do.

No Perlis-specific figures on raids, caning sentences or religious-department activity are sourced, and no source describes entry or visa screening of trans visitors, document checks at the Perlis border with Thailand, or how Malaysian officials treat a passport whose gender marker conflicts with presentation. Those exposure points are not documented either way.

The scope of any federal prosecution against visitors under sections 377A, 377B and the gross-indecency provisions in Perlis specifically is not sourced; the assessment that tourists are rarely targeted rests on the general enforcement pattern described in the national material.
